                               SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                  PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                        §
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                         §
LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                         §
SERVICES CORPORATION TO                           §
AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                       §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                         §     BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST                          §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                     §                     OF
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                          §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,                          §     ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,                        §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,                          §
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,                   §
SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND                        §
WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                               §

 MEWHINNEY FAMILY’S BRIEF ON PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
        REMAND REGARDING PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE 11
               AND PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE 13

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

        Intervenor Ann Mewhinney Matous, individually, and as representative of Kate Richter

Brown, Suzanna Richter, Mary Mewhinney Smith, Madison Goodman, Connor Smith, Miranda

Smith, the Ann Mewhinney Irrevocable Ranch Trust 2024, the Mary Mewhinney Irrevocable

Ranch Trust 2025, and Cathey Creek Limited (collectively, the “Mewhinney Family”), files this

Brief to address two preliminary order issues, namely Preliminary Order Issue 11 and Preliminary

Order Issue 13, filed by the Public Utility Commission in the above referenced docket and shows

as follows:

                                          I. Requested disposition


        The Mewhinney Family requests a supplemental proposal for decision finding that

Applicants have failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state or federal reliability


                                                   1
 standards and have failed to establish estimated consumer congestion cost savings attributable to

the proposed facilities. The ALJs should preserve their determination that need was not established

and recommend denial. The Commission remanded Issues 11 and 13 for express answers. A

reliability label, an ERCOT recommendation, and statewide portfolio figures cannot supply the

missing proof.1


            ERCOT’s own PBRP comparison states that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV alternatives

each meet ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria. Applicants’ discovery responses identify gaps in

the evaluation of Central Texas demand and westward transfers. Gurley’s testimony rests in part

on an assumption that inclusion in the integrated plan establishes the line’s need. The ALJs already

found that the greater weight of credible evidence defeats ERCOT’s recommendation even when

it is afforded great weight. These failures go to the necessity of the proposed facilities, the question

presented by Issue 11.2


            Issue 13 requires its own answer. The PFD found that Applicants did not supply a

quantified estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers. The statewide comparison now

emphasized by Applicants does not allocate savings to Import Path 2. The supplemental PFD

should find that the amount attributable to these facilities has not been established, rather than

substitute the benefits of an entire transmission portfolio for the requested estimate.3

Fact 140 (Aug. 20, 2026), Docket No. 59475, Item 6441 (PFD).

Transmission Plan 345-kV Plan and Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan Comparison at 18–19
(Jan. 2025) (January Comparison).

                                                                    2
                                     II. Scope and burden on remand


        Issue 11 asks whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or

federal reliability standards. Issue 13 asks for estimated congestion cost savings for consumers,

considering current and future expected congestion and the proposed facilities’ ability to reduce

it. The Commission directed SOAH to fully address both questions.4 SOAH Order No. 35 keeps

the evidentiary record closed and requires pinpoint record citations. Applicants’ September 21

directory was accepted as an early-filed brief; it is not a new engineering study.5


        Under PURA § 37.056(a) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b), certification requires a finding of

necessity for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The reliability

provisions require consideration of forecasted load supported by quantifiable evidence.6

Applicants cannot discharge that burden by treating a regional plan’s selection of a project as proof

of every disputed assumption supporting that selection.


        PURA § 37.056(c)(1)–(2) requires consideration of existing service and the need for

additional service; subsection (c-1) addresses historical load, forecasted growth, and loads seeking

interconnection in reliability evaluations. Those statutory factors require examination of the

demand foundation rather than automatic acceptance of a preferred construction plan.7 Rule

25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) expressly requires the forecasted and additional load to be substantiated by

quantifiable evidence. The failures to verify and reconcile the projections bear directly on that

requirement.



4
  Remand Order at 2–3.
5
  SOAH Order No. 35 at 2–3 (Sept. 22, 2026), Docket No. 59475, Item 6597.
6
  16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II).
7
  See PFD at 55–57; Act of May 25, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892 (H.B. 5066), § 1.

                                                        3
         PURA § 39.166 directs regional reliability planning and implementation of necessary

improvements. Former § 39.167 directed development of the Permian plan and expired September

1, 2025. Neither provision prescribed a 765-kV voltage or dispensed with the CCN necessity

determination under § 37.056.8 A statutory instruction to develop a plan cannot be substituted for

proof that these facilities meet the certification criteria.


        The remand calls for findings on the evidence, not an assumption that the reliability

classification decides Issue 11. Nor does exemption from the economic approval tests excuse

answering Issue 13 after the Commission expressly ordered an answer. The Mewhinney Family

requests denial because the reliability necessity showing fails, together with an express finding

that project-attributable consumer congestion savings have not been established.


      III. Issue 11 Applicants have not established necessity under reliability standards


A. ERCOT identified compliant alternatives to the 765 kV plan


        The PBRP’s Table 7.6 answers the threshold voltage question: each studied import-path

option—345 kV, 500 kV, and 765 kV—meets ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria.9 The PBRP

therefore cannot establish that reliability compliance uniquely requires the 765-kV option.

Applicants must supply the missing connection between an identified performance requirement

and the necessity of the facilities for which they seek certification.


        The same table estimates the complete 2038 345-kV alternative at $12.95 billion and the

complete 765-kV alternative at $13.77 billion.10 Those are portfolio construction estimates, but


8
  Act of May 25, 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., ch. 892 (H.B. 5066), § 3; PFD at 54–57.
9
  PBRP at 52.
10
   Id.

                                                        4
 they establish that the PBRP did not reject the 345-kV alternative for failure to meet reliability

criteria and did not identify 765 kV as the lowest-cost compliant portfolio. The claimed necessity

cannot rest on the premise that the PBRP disclosed no compliant lower-voltage alternative.


            The ALJs should expressly find that meeting a reliability standard and selecting a particular

construction plan are separate determinations. Table 7.6 supports the former for multiple plans. It

does not establish the latter for Import Path 2.


B. TPL-001-5.1 does not prescribe this line or this voltage


            The PBRP identifies NERC TPL-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, and ERCOT Planning

Criteria as the framework for its assessments. It describes intact-system and contingency analyses,

normal and emergency thermal ratings, voltage limits, and limited dynamic stability criteria.11

Applicants must connect those requirements to the specific deficiency that allegedly makes Import

Path 2 necessary. Listing contingency categories does not establish that connection.


            TPL-001-5.1 is a transmission system planning performance standard. Requirement R2,

Part 2.7 requires corrective planning when the analysis identifies failure to meet the applicable

Table 1 performance requirements. Part 2.7.1 identifies multiple corrective measures, including

facility modifications, operating procedures, demand-side measures, and new technologies.

Nothing in those provisions prescribes Bell County East–Big Hill, Big Hill–Sand Lake, or a 765-

kV voltage.12




11
     PBRP § 2.5.1 at 13–14.
12
     NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, R2, Parts 2.7–2.7.1 at 5; Table 1 at 21–25.

                                                           5
         Gurley’s reference to N-1 and N-1-1 studies does not fill the project-specific gap. He

testified that he was unaware of a study isolating each line and expressed an assumption about why

multiple lines were recommended.13 The PFD rejected using NERC contingencies as a substitute

for project-specific need.14 The supplemental PFD should retain that distinction and identify the

missing link between the performance obligation and this construction proposal.


        Federal enforceability does not compel approval of this CCN. Applicable entities must

comply with approved reliability standards, and violations may be enforced under 16 U.S.C. §

824o(b)(1),(e). But Congress excludes requirements to enlarge facilities or construct new

transmission capacity from the statutory definition of a reliability standard, and § 215 does not

authorize FERC or the ERO to order additional transmission construction.15 Applicants cannot

turn an enforceable performance obligation into a federal command to approve their selected

project.


C. Great weight does not cure the adverse evidence


        Staff argues that the PFD failed to afford ERCOT’s recommendation great weight.16 That

argument does not answer the ALJs’ alternative determination: even affording great weight to

ERCOT’s recommendation, the greater weight of credible evidence is against it.17 Staff’s

disagreement about deference therefore leaves the adverse evidentiary finding unresolved.




13
   Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:7–45:4.
14
   PFD at 88–89, 180, proposed Finding of Fact 130.
15
   Id. § 824o(a)(3), (i)(2).

6471 (Staff Exceptions).

                                                        6
         The statutory and regulatory inquiry still requires quantifiable support for forecasted

demand and proof of necessity. The PFD explains that the officer-letter and unconfirmed loads

warrant scrutiny under the adjusted forecasting methodology, and that statutory use of the S&P

Global forecast did not itself constitute a credibility determination by ERCOT.18 A

recommendation cannot verify its own disputed inputs merely by being repeated.


        Applicants’ witnesses also lacked firsthand responsibility for significant portions of the

analysis on which the recommendation depends. Martin acknowledged that Applicants did not run

the power flows producing the 2030 exit strategy. Gurley confirmed that ERCOT performed the

studies and supplied the comparison-table figures, and described the limits of his knowledge of

the actual modeling work.19 Those admissions leave the findings dependent on what the underlying

studies actually demonstrate, rather than the witnesses’ repetition of their conclusions.


D. Approval of Import Path 1 does not establish need for Import Path 2


        Staff relies on Commission decisions approving Import Path 1 and reasons that it is “only

logical to conclude” that Import Path 2 is another necessary part of the solution.20 That inference

supplies no study of the proposed facilities, no reconciliation of the disputed load assumptions,

and no finding connecting this path to a particular reliability deficiency.


        A regional need for additional service does not establish the necessity of every proposed

route for supplying it. The Commission remanded Issue 11 for an answer about these facilities. An

analogy to another path cannot answer that question. The ALJs should evaluate the role



18
   PFD at 73–77, 90–92, 181, proposed Findings of Fact 132–140.
19
   Tr. Vol. 4 at 40:3–8, 49:4–21, 50:2–10 (June 10, 2026).
20
   Staff Exceptions at 9–10.

                                                       7
 demonstrated for Import Path 2 in the admitted record and reject an inference of necessity based

simply on another project’s approval.21


E. Applicants did not reconcile Central Texas demand with westward transfers


        Applicants’ actual discovery responses establish the omissions. Response 96 states that

neither Oncor nor ERCOT studies parse out Central Texas’s net generation position under the

requested current and 2030 scenarios. Response 97 states that no determination was made in the

STEP or PBRP studies concerning the requested generation availability and concurrent local

service and westward exports.22


        Response 98 states that Oncor was unaware of the specific scenario in which Central Texas

data-center demand absorbs generation otherwise available for westward export. Response 100

states that Applicants were unaware of the requested sensitivity scenario being studied by

ERCOT.23 These responses identify concrete gaps in the analysis; the ALJs should preserve

proposed Findings of Fact 123–126 reflecting them.24


        These omissions matter because the 2025 RTP identifies Central Texas’s need for

additional import capacity. The PFD cites the report’s discussion of higher projected demand,

imports from north of Austin and the Coast Weather Zone, and the limits of the existing import

 lines.25 Applicants failed to reconcile those conditions with their claim that power can reach the

proposed path in the required quantities while local demand is served.


        Describing Bell County East as a transfer hub certainly does not provide that reconciliation.

The hearing discussion identifies power traversing the node from other parts of the system, but a

hub description is not the missing demonstration of available transfers under simultaneous demand

and contingency conditions.26 The failure is the absence of the identified analysis establishing the

asserted reliability function, not a requirement that every generator supplying the line be located

in Bell County.


F. The forecasts and claimed 2030 need remain inadequately reconciled


        The original PBRP’s EHV analysis was limited to 2038; it expressly did not evaluate the

500-kV and 765-kV options for 2030. It reserved that assessment for the 2024 RTP.27

Consequently, the original PBRP cannot itself establish a 2030 need for the proposed 765-kV

facilities. Applicant demonstrated no bridge from the original study to the claimed in-service

deadline.


        Gurley’s assumption that inclusion in the combined plan establishes the line’s need is not

that bridge. He was unaware of a study isolating each line.28 The 2024 Regional Transmission Plan

(RTP) 345-kV Plan and Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan Comparison (“

January Comparison”) likewise begins with the local Permian projects and all three import paths

Findings of Fact 118–120.

 incorporated in the 765-kV starting case.29 Including a project in the starting configuration does

not, by itself, quantify the consequence of omitting or substituting it.


The PFD also identifies ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter, JKK Panel Ex. 01, as

stating that two of the three import paths were needed by 2030 and prioritizing the northern and

southern paths.30 The ALJs found that need for Import Path 2 by 2030 was not established. 31 The

supplemental PFD should address the basis for any asserted change in timing rather than assume

that the later date asserted by Applicants resolves the earlier sequencing evidence.


        The load assumptions present a separate defect. The PFD identifies Applicants’ failure to

analyze the PBRP forecast under the adjusted realization methodology and discusses the

substantial officer-letter and unconfirmed portions of non-oil-and-gas demand.32 Gurley

acknowledged that he would not characterize Applicants as having verified the referenced

projections beyond customer insight and observed growth.33 Neither rising requests nor a

continuing queue establishes the amount of durable demand required to justify this project.


        The PFD records Poole’s acknowledgment that the application used the old forecasting

methodology and that evolving conditions warrant reevaluation.34 Applicants’ Response 94 further

states that determination of whether the identified loads satisfy SB 6’s site-control and financial-

commitment requirements was not possible until the rulemakings were implemented.35 Applicants

 cannot resolve forecast credibility merely by pointing to the continued appearance of the facilities

in later plans.


G. Later S&P evidence undermines the original oil and gas forecast


        The ALJs found that the PBRP’s oil-and-gas projections came from the 2022 S&P Global

study and that the record contained no evidence ERCOT validated those projections.36 That study

relied on producers’ surveys, hoped-for electrification, and emissions-reduction pledges. The

question is whether those assumptions establish durable grid demand, not whether they describe

an aspiration.37


        The PFD expressly addresses S&P Global’s October 2025 analysis reporting a substantial

decline in absolute Permian emissions despite increased production. Based on that later analysis

and Green’s testimony, the ALJs concluded that the premise that producers had to electrify to

reduce absolute emissions had been disproved and that the earlier load forecasts were overstated

and outdated.38 Those findings directly undermine the demand foundation Applicants seek to carry

forward unchanged.


        The ALJs also relied on the materially different oil-and-gas outlook reflected in ERCOT’s

later forecast and the 2025 RTP.39 The supplemental PFD should retain the finding that changed

circumstances defeat the asserted demand justification.40 Applicants cannot reconcile the later

 evidence with the old assumptions and therefore, Applicant’s assumptions cannot establish this

project’s necessity.


H. The Commission ordered a forecast adjustment after the hearing


        The PFD records a further development after the hearing: on June 18, 2026, the

Commission adopted the Batch Zero Base Load adjustment methodology in Project No. 59772.

The PFD quotes the Order Granting Adjustment Request as recognizing that adjusting the Long-

Term Load Forecast “to a more realistic value may be warranted.”41 This is a concrete Commission

action addressing forecast realism, not merely an intervenor’s disagreement with ERCOT.


        That action reinforces the need to reconcile the original demand assumptions with the

changed forecasting framework. Continued reliance on the PBRP’s earlier load projections cannot

answer the Commission’s concern about realism. The studies Applicant offered to establish Import

Path 2’s necessity do not incorporate the relevant adjusted demand and therefore do not identify

any demonstrated necessity remaining after the adjustment.42 A repeated recommendation does

not resolve that evidentiary question.


I. GTC references do not establish the missing necessity showing


        The ALJs separately considered the Far West Import GTC material and found that it did

not validate the original load forecast or establish Import Path 2’s necessity. The April 2026

presentation listed the Permian import paths as one of seven upgrades characterized as helping to

exit the constraints.43 The supplemental PFD should retain the distinction between a transmission

 constraint and verification of the demand assumptions used to justify a particular corrective

investment.


           Applicants’ Response 93 asserts that reduced-load sensitivities and existing constraints

establish continued need, but does not set out the scenario results or identify a calculation isolating

this path’s necessity.44 An assertion of a sensitivity result is not an explanation of the modeled load

composition, the omitted or substituted facilities, or the performance requirement remaining

unsatisfied. The ALJs should identify those results in the admitted evidence before treating the

assertion as an answer to the forecast, timing, and project-specific gaps.


J. The reliability exemption cannot substitute for the finding it requires


           Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(I) exempts qualifying reliability projects from the economic tests.

It does not eliminate the necessity determination presented by Issue 11. Applicants must show why

the proposed facilities are necessary to meet the identified reliability requirements. The record

deficiencies discussed above prevent a finding based solely on the project’s classification.


           Intervenor requests an express answer to Issue 11 that Applicants have not established the

proposed facilities’ necessity to meet state or federal reliability standards. The ALJs should retain

their adverse assessment of the evidence, including their finding against the recommendation even

when given great weight, and recommend denial.45




44
     Howton Ex. JAH-32 at 9–10.

           IV. Issue 13 Applicants have not established consumer congestion savings


A. The original PFD identified the missing estimate


        The PFD found that Applicants did not submit estimated congestion cost savings to

consumers and that the record contained no evidence quantifying the requested amount.46 The

Commission has now required an express answer to Issue 13.47 The supplemental PFD should

preserve the factual deficiency and answer the question directly.


        A reliability classification does not generate a savings estimate. Nor can the exemption

from the economic approval tests be used to avoid the Commission’s remand instruction. The ALJs

should find that a quantified estimate attributable to these facilities has not been established and

identify the limits of the portfolio figures cited in place of it.


B. Statewide figures do not quantify savings from Import Path 2


        The January Comparison evaluates complete statewide transmission portfolios using 2034

and 2039 economic cases. Its method adds each full plan to the economic base cases, and Tables

1.3.2 and 1.3.3 report statewide outcomes.48 The tables do not allocate those outcomes to Import

Path 2. They therefore do not establish the amount of consumer congestion savings caused by these

proposed facilities.




46
   PFD at 149–150, 191, proposed Findings of Fact 226–227.
47
   Remand Order at 2–3.
48

                                                      14
         The 2025 RTP material cited in Applicants’ directory likewise begins its economic case

with the 765-kV STEP included.49 Assuming an installed transmission configuration does not

identify the incremental savings from approving this CCN.


        There is no allocation in the cited tables by project, and no basis in them for dividing the

statewide totals by mileage, construction cost, or the number of import paths. The requested

finding must concern the facilities before the ALJs. Substitution of a portfolio total would attribute

benefits without the supporting calculation.


C. The 2034 consumer result defeats an unqualified superiority claim


        For 2034, ERCOT reports $136 million less system-wide consumer energy cost savings

for the 765-kV portfolio than for the 345-kV portfolio, expressed in 2025 dollars.50 That result is

specific to the modeled 2034 comparison. It defeats any unqualified claim that the 765-kV choice

produces greater consumer savings in every modeled year and reinforces the need to identify

precisely which output is being used to answer Issue 13.


        The tables separately report production costs, consumer energy costs, and congestion rent.

Those outputs cannot be relabeled interchangeably or combined without a supported explanation

of overlap and consumer effects.51 A reduction in portfolio congestion rent is not, without the

missing analysis, a quantified reduction in consumer bills attributable to this project.


D. The study assumptions and witness testimony do not supply the calculation

          The January Comparison’s economic cases omit the officer-letter large loads unavailable

when its base cases were developed.52 Its economic scenarios therefore do not use the same

demand assumptions as the reliability showing. Applicants must explain the relevance of those

economic outputs to the proposed facilities and their asserted service date rather than use the

differing cases as interchangeable evidence.


         Martin testified that his rebuttal did not address project costs or compare Import Path 2’s

costs with alternatives. Gurley confirmed that ERCOT supplied the comparison-table figures and

that he did not independently calculate them.53 Neither statement supplies the project-attributable

consumer congestion calculation required by Issue 13.


         Historical ERCOT-wide congestion rent totals also cannot answer the question. The

January Comparison reports $2.3 billion for 2023 and $1.97 billion for 2024, but those figures are

system totals rather than estimates of congestion costs avoided by these facilities.54 The missing

showing concerns the share affected by the project, its expected reduction under the studied

conditions, and the amount reaching consumers.


E. Requested answer to Issue 13


         The Mewhinney Family requests an express finding that Applicants have not established a

quantified estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to Import Path 2. The

statewide tables, historical totals, and witness references do not supply that estimate. The amount

should be described as unestablished; an unsupported dollar amount should not be assigned to the



52
   January Comparison at ii, 18.
53
   Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10–17, 49:10–21.
54
   January Comparison at iv.

                                                 16
 proposed facilities. This answers the remanded question and prevents portfolio figures from

concealing the project-specific omission.


                                V. Requested findings and conclusions


1. The PBRP identifies the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import-path alternatives as meeting

ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria.55 Compliance does not uniquely establish necessity for the

proposed 765-kV facilities.


2. Applicants’ Central Texas responses identify the missing regional generation determination and

the specific concurrent-demand and sensitivity scenarios of which they were unaware.56 The

proposed findings addressing those omissions should be retained.57


3. The original PBRP’s EHV evaluation concerns 2038, not 2030.58 The evidence discussed in the

PFD did not establish Import Path 2’s necessity by 2030.59


4. The greater weight of credible evidence is against ERCOT’s recommendation even when

afforded great weight.60 Neither deference nor another path’s approval resolves the deficiencies

identified for Import Path 2.

 5. NERC performance obligations and contingency requirements do not prescribe this line or

voltage.61 Applicants have not established the connection required for an affirmative answer to

Issue 11.


6. The January Comparison reports statewide portfolio outcomes without allocating consumer

congestion savings to Import Path 2.62 Applicants have not established the quantified project-

attributable estimate requested by Issue 13.63


         The Mewhinney Family requests conclusions that Applicants have failed to establish

necessity under Issue 11; that a reliability designation and great-weight treatment do not cure the

identified failures of proof; and that Issue 13 must be expressly answered with a finding that the

project-attributable consumer congestion savings amount has not been established.


                                                    VI. Prayer


         The Mewhinney Family respectfully requests that the ALJs issue a supplemental or

amended PFD expressly answering Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13; find that Applicants have

not established that the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability

standards; find that estimated consumer congestion savings attributable to these facilities have not

been established; preserve the adverse findings on need supported by the record; and recommend

denial of the applications comprising Import Path 2. The Mewhinney Family requests all further

relief within the scope of remand to which they are entitled.

                                     II. Scope and burden on remand


        Issue 11 asks whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or

federal reliability standards. Issue 13 asks for estimated congestion cost savings for consumers,

considering current and future expected congestion and the proposed facilities' ability to reduce

it. The Commission directed SOAH to fully address both questions.4 SOAH Order No. 35 keeps

the evidentiary record closed and requires pinpoint record citations. Applicants' September 21

directory was accepted as an early-filed brief; it is not a new engineering study.5


        Under PURA § 37.056(a) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b), certification requires a finding of

necessity for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The reliability

provisions require consideration of forecasted load supported by quantifiable evidence.6

Applicants cannot discharge that burden by treating a regional plan's selection of a project as proof

of every disputed assumption supporting that selection.


        PURA § 37.056(c)(1)-(2) requires consideration of existing service and the need for

additional service; subsection (c-1) addresses historical load, forecasted growth, and loads seeking

interconnection in reliability evaluations. Those statutory factors require examination of the

demand foundation rather than automatic acceptance of a preferred construction plan.7 Rule

25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) expressly requires the forecasted and additional load to be substantiated by

quantifiable evidence. The failures to verify and reconcile the projections bear directly on that

requirement.

      III. Issue 11 Applicants have not established necessity under reliability standards


A. ERCOT identified compliant alternatives to the 765 kV plan


        The PBRP' s Table 7.6 answers the threshold voltage question: each studied import-path

option-345 kV, 500 kV, and 765 kV-meets ERCOT and NERC reliability criteria.' The PBRP

therefore cannot establish that reliability compliance uniquely requires the 765-kV option.

Applicants must supply the missing connection between an identified performance requirement

and the necessity of the facilities for which they seek certification.


        The same table estimates the complete 2038 345-kV alternative at $12.95 billion and the

complete 765-kV alternative at $13.77 billion.10 Those are portfolio construction estimates, but

B. TPL-001-5.1 does not prescribe this line or this voltage


        The PBRP identifies NERC TPL-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, and ERCOT Planning

Criteria as the framework for its assessments. It describes intact-system and contingency analyses,

normal and emergency thermal ratings, voltage limits, and limited dynamic stability criteria. 11

Applicants must connect those requirements to the specific deficiency that allegedly makes Import

Path 2 necessary. Listing contingency categories does not establish that connection.


        TPL-001-5.1 is a transmission system planning performance standard. Requirement R2,

Part 2.7 requires corrective planning when the analysis identifies failure to meet the applicable

Table 1 performance requirements. Part 2.7.1 identifies multiple corrective measures, including

facility modifications, operating procedures, demand-side measures, and new technologies.

Nothing in those provisions prescribes Bell County East-Big Hill, Big Hill-Sand Lake, or a 765-

kV voltage.12

           IV. Issue 13 Applicants have not established consumer congestion savings


A. The original PFD identified the missing estimate


        The PFD found that Applicants did not submit estimated congestion cost savings to

consumers and that the record contained no evidence quantifying the requested amount.46 The

Commission has now required an express answer to Issue 13.47 The supplemental PFD should

preserve the factual deficiency and answer the question directly.


        A reliability classification does not generate a savings estimate. Nor can the exemption

from the economic approval tests be used to avoid the Commission's remand instruction. The ALJs

should find that a quantified estimate attributable to these facilities has not been established and

identify the limits of the portfolio figures cited in place of it.


B. Statewide figures do not quantify savings from Import Path 2


        The January Comparison evaluates complete statewide transmission portfolios using 2034

and 2039 economic cases. Its method adds each full plan to the economic base cases, and Tables

1.3.2 and 1.3.3 report statewide outcomes.48 The tables do not allocate those outcomes to Import

Path 2. They therefore do not establish the amount of consumer congestion savings caused by these

proposed facilities.

         The 2025 RTP material cited in Applicants' directory likewise begins its economic case

with the 765-kV STEP included.49 Assuming an installed transmission configuration does not

identify the incremental savings from approving this CCN.


        There is no allocation in the cited tables by project, and no basis in them for dividing the

statewide totals by mileage, construction cost, or the number of import paths. The requested

finding must concern the facilities before the ALJs. Substitution of a portfolio total would attribute

benefits without the supporting calculation.


C. The 2034 consumer result defeats an unqualified superiority claim


        For 2034, ERCOT reports $136 million less system-wide consumer energy cost savings

for the 765-kV portfolio than for the 345-kV portfolio, expressed in 2025 dollars.50 That result is

specific to the modeled 2034 comparison. It defeats any unqualified claim that the 765-kV choice

produces greater consumer savings in every modeled year and reinforces the need to identify

precisely which output is being used to answer Issue 13.


        The tables separately report production costs, consumer energy costs, and congestion rent.

Those outputs cannot be relabeled interchangeably or combined without a supported explanation

of overlap and consumer effects.51 A reduction in portfolio congestion rent is not, without the

missing analysis, a quantified reduction in consumer bills attributable to this project.
